The Value of More Than One Voice

When I was deciding which high school elective to take last spring, I asked my older cousin, who told me to take computer science because "that's where the jobs are." If I had stopped there, I would have signed up without a second thought. Instead, I also asked my art teacher, my best friend, and my mom. Each one told me something different, and by the end I understood my own choice far better than I would have from one conversation. That experience taught me something many people learn the hard way: asking more than one person for advice usually leads to a better decision. Multiple opinions help because they reveal blind spots, balance out personal bias, and give the person asking a fuller picture of what the choice really involves.

The first reason to seek several opinions is that every person sees only part of a situation. No one has lived every life or tried every path, so their advice comes from their own narrow experience. My cousin loved computer science because he was good at math and enjoyed puzzles. His advice was honest, but it fit him, not necessarily me. When I talked to my art teacher, she pointed out that I spent most of my free time drawing and that the digital design class combined art with technology. I had never even considered that option. One advisor showed me one door; the second showed me a door I did not know existed. When people gather advice from several sources, those partial views start to overlap and form something closer to the whole truth.

A second reason is that everyone carries some bias, even when they mean well. Parents may want their children to choose the safe option because they worry. Friends may want you to choose whatever keeps you close to them. A salesperson wants you to buy the product they are selling. None of these people are necessarily lying, but their wishes can quietly shape what they say. Consider someone buying a used car. If they only ask the dealer, they will hear that the car is in great shape and a good deal. If they also ask a mechanic friend to look under the hood and check online reviews from other owners, they may learn that the model has a common transmission problem. By hearing from people with different interests, the buyer can spot where one opinion leans too far in one direction and adjust for it.

Third, hearing different opinions forces a person to think harder about their own values. When two trusted people disagree, you cannot simply follow orders; you have to ask yourself which reasoning makes more sense and what matters most to you. When my mom told me to pick the class with the easiest grading so I could protect my GPA, and my friend told me to pick whatever sounded the most fun, I realized I had to decide for myself whether I cared more about grades or enjoyment. That question was uncomfortable, but answering it made me more confident in the final choice. A single piece of advice can make a decision feel easy, but it can also let someone avoid the real thinking the decision requires.

Seeking multiple opinions also protects against simple mistakes. Doctors understand this well, which is why patients facing serious surgery are often encouraged to get a second opinion. A second doctor may read the same test results differently, suggest a less risky treatment, or confirm that the first diagnosis was correct. Either way, the patient benefits. If the doctors agree, the patient can move forward with greater trust. If they disagree, the patient has discovered an important question before it was too late. The same idea applies in smaller situations, such as asking two teachers to read a college essay before submitting it. One might catch a confusing sentence the other missed.

Of course, gathering advice from too many people can become overwhelming, and in the end the decision still belongs to the person making it. Advice is a tool, not a replacement for judgment. The goal is not to count votes and go with the majority, but to collect enough perspectives to make an informed choice. Choosing advisors who know different things, such as an expert, someone who has lived through a similar situation, and someone who knows you personally, often works better than asking ten people with the same background.

In the end, I chose the digital design class, and it turned out to be my favorite course of the year. I would never have found it if I had trusted only my first piece of advice. Talking to several people helped me see more options, notice hidden biases, and understand what I truly wanted. Whether someone is choosing a class, a car, or a medical treatment, listening to more than one voice gives them the best chance of choosing well.
